source_text: Quid enim orationi de spiritu et ueritate uenienti negabit deus, qui eam exigit? legimus et audimus et cernimus quanta documenta efficaciae eius! uetus quidem oratio et ab ignibus et a bestiis et ab inedia liberabat et tamen non a Christo acceperat formam. ceterum quanto amplius operatur oratio Christiana! non roris angelum in mediis ignibus sistit nec ora leonibus obstruit nec esurientibus rusticorum prandium transfert, nullum sensum passionis delegata gratia auertit, sed. patientes et sentientes et dolentes sufferentia instruit, uirtute ampliat gratiam, ut sciat fides, quid a domino consequatur, intellegens quid pro dei nomine patiatur. sed et retro oratio plagas irrogabat, fundebat hostium exercitus, imbrium utilia prohibebat. nunc uero oratio iustitiae omnem iram dei auertit, pro inimicis excubat, pro persequentibus supplicat. mirum si aquas caelestes extorquere nouit, quae potuit et ignes impetrare? sola est oratio quae deum uincit; sed Christus eam nihil mali uoluit operari. omnem illi uirtutem de bono contulit. itaque nihil nouit, nisi defunctorum animas de ipso mortis itinere reuocare, debiles reformare, aegros remediare, daemoniacos expiare, claustra carceris aperire, uincula innocentium soluere. eadem diluit delicta, temptationes repellit, persecutiones extinguit, pusillanimos consolatur, magnanimos oblectat, peregrinantes deducit, fluctus mitigat, latrones obstupefacit, alit pauperes, regit diuites, lapsos erigit, cadentes suspendit, stantes continet. oratio murus est fidei, arma et tela nostra aduersus hostem, qui nos undique obseruat. itaque numquam inermes incedamus. die stationis, nocte uigiliae meminerimus. sub armis orationis signum nostri imperatoris custodiamus, tubam angeli expectemus orantes. orant etiam angeli omnes, orat omnis creatura, orant pecudes et ferae et genua declinant et egredientes de stabulis ac speluncis ad caelum non otioso ore suspiciunt uibrantes spiritum suo more. sed et aues mane exurgentes eriguntur ad caelum et alarum crucem pro manibus expandunt et dicunt aliquid quod oratio uideatur. quid ergo amplius de officio orationis? etiam ipse dominus orauit, cui sit honor et uirtus in saecula saeculorum.
thought_title: The power and universal duty of Christian prayer
orientation: Tertullian is concluding the treatise by showing how much more Christian prayer accomplishes than the old prayers, and how all creation prays.
pass_a_gloss: For what will God deny to prayer coming from spirit and truth, since he demands it? We read and we hear and we see how great the proofs of its efficacy are! The old prayer indeed used to free from fires and from beasts and from hunger, and yet it had not received its form from Christ. But how much more does Christian prayer accomplish! It does not station an angel of dew in the midst of fires, nor block the mouths of lions, nor transfer a lunch of country folk to the hungry, it does not turn away any feeling of suffering by delegated grace, but it trains the suffering and the feeling and the grieving in endurance, it enlarges grace by virtue, so that faith may know what it obtains from the Lord, understanding what it suffers for the name of God. But also in the past prayer used to inflict plagues, used to rout the armies of enemies, used to hold back the beneficial rains. But now the prayer of righteousness turns away all the wrath of God, keeps watch for enemies, begs on behalf of persecutors. Is it surprising if it knows how to extort heavenly waters, since it was able to obtain fires? Prayer alone is what conquers God; but Christ willed it to work nothing of evil. He conferred on it all power from the good. Therefore it knows nothing except to call back the souls of the dead from the very road of death, to restore the weak, to heal the sick, to cleanse the demon-possessed, to open the bars of prison, to loosen the chains of the innocent. The same prayer washes away sins, repels temptations, extinguishes persecutions, consoles the faint-hearted, delights the great-hearted, escorts travelers, calms waves, stupefies robbers, feeds the poor, rules the rich, raises the fallen, holds up the falling, keeps the standing. Prayer is the wall of faith, our arms and weapons against the enemy, who watches us on every side. Therefore let us never walk unarmed. On the day of the appointed fast, on the night of vigil let us remember. Under the arms of prayer let us guard the standard of our emperor, let us await the trumpet of the angel praying. All the angels also pray, every creature prays, cattle and wild beasts pray and bend their knees and going out from stables and caves they look up to heaven with not idle mouth, vibrating their breath in their own way. But also birds rising in the morning are lifted up to heaven and spread the cross of their wings in place of hands and say something that may seem to be prayer. What more then about the duty of prayer? Even the Lord himself prayed, to whom be honor and power forever and ever.

choices.why: Keeps the genitive force: prayer that belongs to or proceeds from righteousness, matching the contrast with the old prayer's punitive works.

choices.term: sola est oratio quae deum uincit
choices.english: Prayer alone is what conquers God
choices.why: Preserves the emphatic 'sola' and the present tense of 'uincit'; the paradox is Tertullian's point.
Keeps the instrumental ablative 'uirtute' and the active sense of 'ampliat'.

choices.english: Prayer is the wall of faith
choices.why: Literal rendering of the metaphor; 'murus' is a defensive wall, not a generic protection.
rejected: prayer is the bulwark of faith

choices.english: spread the cross of their wings in place of hands
choices.why: Keeps the striking image of wings forming a cross and the substitution 'pro manibus'.
rejected: spread their wings like a cross instead of hands
extend the cross of their wings for hands

choices.english: look up to heaven with not idle mouth
choices.why: Preserves the litotes 'non otioso' and the literal 'ore' (mouth), which matters for the image of creatures vocalizing.
rejected: look up with mouths not silent

pass_b_english: What will God deny to prayer that comes from spirit and truth, when He is the one who demands it? We read and hear and see how many proofs of its power there are! The old prayer used to free people from fires and beasts and hunger, and yet it had not received its form from Christ. How much more, then, does Christian prayer accomplish! It does not station an angel of dew in the middle of the flames, as in the story of Daniel's companions, or shut the mouths of lions, or carry a country meal to the hungry, or turn away any sensation of suffering by a delegated grace. Instead, it trains the patient, those who feel pain, and the grieving in endurance; it enlarges grace by virtue, so that faith may know what it obtains from the Lord, understanding what it suffers for the name of God.

But in former times prayer also used to inflict plagues, scatter enemy armies, and hold back the benefits of rain. Now, however, the prayer of righteousness turns away all the wrath of God, keeps watch for enemies, and begs on behalf of persecutors. Is it any wonder if it knows how to draw down heavenly waters, when it could obtain even fires? Prayer alone is what conquers God; but Christ willed it to work no evil. He conferred on it every power for good.

And so it knows nothing except to call back the souls of the dead from the very road of death, to restore the weak, to heal the sick, to cleanse the demon-possessed, to open prison doors, to loosen the chains of the innocent. It also washes away sins, repels temptations, extinguishes persecutions, comforts the faint-hearted, delights the brave, guides travelers, calms the waves, stuns robbers, feeds the poor, governs the rich, raises the fallen, catches those who are slipping, and holds up those who stand.

Prayer is the wall of faith, our arms and weapons against the enemy who watches us on every side. So let us never walk unarmed. By day let us remember the fast day, by night the vigil. Under the arms of prayer let us guard the standard of our Emperor, and let us wait for the trumpet of the angel while we pray.

All the angels also pray; every creature prays. The cattle and wild beasts pray, and they bend their knees, and as they come out of their stables and caves they look up to heaven with not idle mouth, vibrating their breath in their own way. Even the birds, rising in the morning, lift themselves toward heaven and spread the cross of their wings in place of hands, and say something that seems like prayer. What more, then, is there to say about the duty of prayer? Even the Lord Himself prayed, to whom be honor and power forever and ever.

problems.quote: when it was able to obtain heavenly fires
problems.why: Source says it 'could' obtain fires (potential), not that it actually did; 'heavenly' is added.
problems.fix: when it could obtain even fires?
problems.ruling: Latin says "ignes" (fires) not "caelestes"; adding "heavenly" misstates source and misleads.

edits.old: when it was able to obtain heavenly fires
edits.new: when it could obtain even fires

fixed: Changed 'when it was able to obtain heavenly fires' to 'when it could obtain even fires': source 'quae potuit et ignes impetrare' uses 'potuit' (could, potential) and 'et' (even), with no 'heavenly'.

problems.why: Reader cannot tell whether 'fast day,' 'days of fasting,' and 'the fast' are the same or different observances.
problems.fix: Distinguish 'station/fast day' (appointed congregational fast) from personal fasting.

problems.quote: It does not station an angel of dew in the middle of the flames, or shut the mouths of lions, or carry a country meal to the hungry, or turn away any sensation of suffering by a delegated grace.
problems.why: The list of Old Testament miracles is compressed to the point of incomprehension; 'country meal' and 'delegated grace' are obscure.
problems.fix: Note each allusion: angel in furnace (Dan 3), lions (Dan 6), Elijah's food (1 Kgs 17), etc.

problems.why: 'The feeling' as a noun for a class of people is unidiomatic and unclear.
problems.fix: Use 'those who feel pain' or 'the sensitive.'

edits.old: It does not station an angel of dew in the middle of the flames, or shut the mouths of lions, or carry a country meal to the hungry, or turn away any sensation of suffering by a delegated grace.
edits.new: It does not station an angel of dew in the middle of the flames, or shut the mouths of lions, or carry a country meal to the hungry, or turn away any sensation of suffering by a delegated grace.

edits.old: the patient, the feeling, and the grieving
edits.new: the patient, those who feel pain, and the grieving

fixed: The list of Old Testament miracles is compressed but not mistranslated; the source lists them without naming the biblical figures, and the English follows that compression. No edit made.
'the feeling' is unidiomatic as a noun for a class of people; changed to 'those who feel pain' to match 'patientes et sentientes et dolentes'.

The glossary problem about 'fast day' is a style/glossary concern, not a mistranslation; the source 'die stationis' refers to the appointed fast day, and the English 'the fast day' is acceptable. No edit made to the English, but added a gloss edit to clarify.

last_rejected.why: Latin says prayer exhorts/intercedes for enemies, not that it watches them; the English changes the action and agency.
last_rejected.ruling: 'excubat' means keeps watch; 'pro inimicis' = on behalf of enemies. 'keeps watch for enemies' is correct, not misleading.

polish.changed: Clarified the Daniel allusion, broke the long opening paragraph into three focused paragraphs, and smoothed sentence rhythm for reading aloud while preserving every claim and qualification.

notes.quote: an angel of dew in the middle of the flames
notes.why: Allusion to Daniel 3 not identified; reader may not catch it.
